source.title: Random features and polynomial rules
source.authors: Fabián Aguirre-López; Silvio Franz; Mauro Pastore

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double-descent-related behavior in random-features models using a replica-theory analysis and synthetic numerical experiments, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own generalization-error results as feature count or training-set size varies, and its explicit statement about regularization and peak sharpness. Results cited from other work are not rows. The activation-function comparison about learning cubic features is not a double-descent result.
record.test_reason: The study computes generalization curves of random-features models with replica theory and checks them against ridge-regression simulations. It sweeps feature count N and sample count P and finds interpolation peaks at N∼P. Its results bear directly on model-wise double descent in a non-deep model class (V4), sample-wise non-monotonicity (V3), and regularization dependence and multiple peaks (V6). The RFM has a fixed random first layer and only a trained readout, so it is not a deep network trained end to end (V1). Random features are also one of the model classes in an original source (arXiv:1812.11118), so this is a different method, replica theory, applied to a related setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the RFM learns as an equivalent polynomial model whose degree is set by log N/log D, plus an effective noise term from higher-order kernel components. That noise term produces a regularization-dependent interpolation peak at N∼P. The theory matches simulations over many orders of magnitude, but only qualitatively near the peak in some cases. They also stress that when the teacher is simpler than the network, overfitting peaks appear and overparametrization is not always optimal.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes random-features models using a replica-based effective polynomial theory and synthetic numerical experiments; it is not a reproduction of the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The interpolation peak depends on weight regularization: the authors state that lower ζ makes it sharper. The reported results also vary with training-set size, feature count, teacher complexity, and activation function.

fits_no_version.finding: For a cubic teacher, a ReLU student cannot learn cubic features because its Hermite coefficient µ3=0, so error stays at 1/2; an ELU student can learn them (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learnability of order-ℓ features in random-features models requires a nonzero ℓ-th Hermite coefficient of the activation.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning curves versus P show a staircase, learning order-K features at P∼D^K, whenever N≫P (Figs. 1, 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel and random-features learning curves descend in steps at polynomial sample scales.

record.peer_reviewed: SciPost Physics submission; publication information is stated to appear upon publication.
record.problems: The analysis relies on Gaussian and replica-symmetry assumptions and approximations involving kernel truncation and orthogonal row spaces. The authors report that quantitative agreement is weaker near the interpolation peak in some cases. Numerical experiments average over instances, but the text does not report uncertainty intervals or error bars.
record.rows_left_out: No additional double-descent result rows were left out. Figure 4's activation-function comparison concerns learning cubic teacher features, not the claim versions.

untested.parts: No deep or end-to-end trained networks; only random-features models with a trained readout.
No sweep over training time or epochs; the solution is closed-form ridge regression.
Only synthetic Gaussian-input polynomial-teacher tasks; no real data or deep models.
Only one model class (RFM); the study does not compare across model classes or show the curve subsuming the classical U-shape.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
Label noise is not varied (the classification teachers are deterministic). Optimally tuned regularization is not shown to remove the peak. Multiple peaks along the model-size axis are not examined.
Effective-parameter recounting is not tested. The equivalent polynomial degree is not used to recast the second descent as a U-curve.

missing.what: Mechanism claim bearing on V6: higher-order Hermite terms act as effective noise, and this produces the N∼P interpolation peak. A vanilla polynomial student would show no peak.
Teacher–student overlaps of already-learned features become noisy in the interpolation regime (Fig. 1 right). This is a variance signature at the peak.

record.verdict_notes: R6 was extended to V6 for multiple descent along the sample axis. The V4 verdict was split: R3 and R4 are limits_scope because the overall optimum is underparametrized. The V6 regularization evidence is theoretical (R8). Random features also appear in the Belkin et al. original, so V4 support here extends that setting with a different method rather than a new model class. All rows are figure-only; no numerical values are readable from the text.

versions.untested_parts: The size sweeps are for random-features models, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or time.
The reported data sweeps use synthetic teacher-student settings, not other data or model settings.
The reported experiments concern random-features models; the study does not test the claim across multiple model classes or establish that it subsumes the classical U-shaped curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study reports regularization dependence of peak sharpness, but does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether model-size curves split into multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The equivalent polynomial representation is not used to recast the second descent as an ordinary U-shaped curve against an effective parameter count.

relationships.condition: RFM N sweeps with a quadratic teacher (P=10^4) and a linear teacher with small data (P=40)
relationships.reason: Error peaks at N∼P and falls again with more features, and for P=40 the optimum lies in the overparametrized regime (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Error peaked at N≈P and declined with more features, with the optimum beyond interpolation for P=40.

relationships.condition: Linear teacher with P=200 and P=400, ζ=10^-4
relationships.reason: The second descent occurs, but the minimum-error N is underparametrized. The authors state that overparametrization is not always optimal when the teacher is simpler than the network (R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: The second descent occurred, but the error-minimizing N was underparameterized, so overparameterization was not always optimal for a simpler teacher.

relationships.condition: Synthetic RFM teacher-student classification, quadratic and linear teachers
relationships.reason: Error rises with P near the interpolation peak at P∼N (R5, R6). At fixed N past the peak, P=400 gives higher error than P=200 (R7).
relationships.display_finding: Error rose near P ∼ N, and at fixed N beyond the peak, P = 400 gave higher error than P = 200.

relationships.condition: Linear-teacher P sweep, and the asymptotic regime N∼P∼D^L
relationships.reason: The P sweep shows multiple peaks, at P∼D² and at P∼N (R6). The theory states the interpolation peak sharpens as ζ decreases (R8, a theory result).
relationships.display_finding: Peaks appeared at P∼D² and P∼N, and theory predicted a sharper interpolation peak as ζ decreased.
